honesty_statement.summary: Every recovery figure in this project's Phase 7 reports is a simulated outcome scored by a seeded, hand-built oracle, never an observed real-world rupee. This document measures policy quality against a known, stated, adversarially-inspectable world -- not real recovery -- and says so before presenting a single number.
points: Recovery outcomes are simulated by a seeded oracle (reflow.outcome.oracle.RecoveryOracle), never observed from real customers or a live Razorpay payment succeeding or failing for a real commercial reason.

What is measured is policy quality against a known-ground-truth world, not real-world rupees: every 'money recovered' figure is the sum of amounts the oracle decided would recover, under probabilities this project itself assigned and disclosed.

The oracle exists because Razorpay's test mode exposes only a binary pass/fail toggle per payment, not a probability -- there is no sandbox surface that reports 'a card_declined failure recovers 42% of the time given a fresh Payment Link.' A realistic, multi-reason outcome model cannot be obtained from the sandbox; it can only be assumed, honestly and on the record, or not built at all.

Oracle probabilities derive from Razorpay's own vendored Next Steps remediation classes (reflow.taxonomy.remediation.RemediationClass), not invented per-reason-code numbers -- two free parameters per class (a no-action self-recovery floor and a textbook-action ceiling), never per reason code, and never tuned after seeing a simulation result.

Results are reported across a three-point sensitivity band (pessimistic / central / optimistic) precisely so no single assumed probability carries the project's conclusion -- every headline claim below is checked against whether it holds at every point in that band, not only at the central estimate.

what_this_means: reflow never recovers more absolute rupees than the naive, unbounded notify_all baseline, at any point in the sensitivity band -- that comparison is reported honestly as a loss, not reframed. That is not true of notify_all_once, the more realistic single-shot chase baseline: reflow recovers 95.0-97.1% of notify_all's rupees while sending 28.4-28.9% fewer contacts than notify_all, and against notify_all_once the range is 98.8-101.0%, not symmetric around 100% -- at the pessimistic level reflow recovers MORE absolute money than notify_all_once (48,701,612 vs. 48,242,292 rupees, 100.95%), and only at central (98.83%) and optimistic (99.91%) does it recover slightly less. This is stated plainly rather than only reporting the two points that show a loss, per this project's first governing principle: a result in this project's own favour is reported with the same rigor as one against it. reflow is also always cheaper per rupee recovered than both chase baselines, by roughly 25-26%. The correct reading is comparable-to-better recovery against the realistic chase baseline, and materially lower customer-contact cost against both chase baselines, robust across the whole plausible probability band -- not a win on the single metric of total rupees recovered against notify_all specifically, which remains a loss and is reported as one.

guardrail_opportunity_cost_analysis.methodology: For every reflow decision where a guardrail changed an escalatable candidate action (recovery_link_now / recovery_link_backoff / switch_method / escalate_human) into a non-escalatable final action, this analysis additionally scores the same payment attempt's SAME deterministic oracle draw against the pre-guardrail candidate action, using reflow.outcome.oracle.RecoveryOracle.sample_recovery -- the identical mechanism reflow.eval.simulate already uses, since the oracle's draw is shared across actions by design (see reflow.outcome.oracle module docstring) specifically so this kind of counterfactual comparison is well-defined and monotonic. This is a one-off, read-only analysis script built for this report from existing public reflow APIs; it does not modify reflow.eval.simulate or its committed report.
guardrail_opportunity_cost_analysis.interpretation: At the central estimate, roughly 15.5% of the 9,992 guardrail-blocked chase/escalation events (1,552 events, 1,548 distinct orders) would have recovered under the same oracle had the guardrail not intervened; 1,487 orders (3.3% of all 44,674 orders in the corpus) never recovered by any other path in the simulation as a result. This is the concrete, measured size of the deliberate trade-off reflow's guardrails make -- fewer contacts, and a real, non-zero, quantified number of foregone recoveries among them, not a hidden cost.

model_comparison_summary.selection_rule: Pre-committed: among models with zero call errors, pick the lowest total measured cost, tie-broken by lower mean latency.
model_comparison_summary.surprising_finding: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash is roughly 35x cheaper than google/gemini-3.7-flash and had a perfect first-attempt JSON validity rate, but it was NOT the fastest model measured: its mean latency (20.3s) was the highest of the three, with individual calls ranging from 3.0s to 64.8s, despite reasoning being disabled. google/gemini-3.7-flash, despite mandatory reasoning (3136 reasoning tokens total), had the lowest and tightest mean latency (6.7s, range 3.2-14.5s). All three models reached perfect agreement with Tier 1's deterministic table on every sampled already-resolved reason code, which is independent corroboration that those reasons really are unambiguous, not merely unambiguous to this project's own rule-based parser.
